body_markdown:
Consumers in three states are being urged to check their refrigerators and food-service supplies after a Houston-based food company recalled certain salsa and pico de gallo products because of a potential Salmonella contamination concern.


Ron's Home Style Foods has recalled a combined 4,540 pounds of two products, Salsa Autentica and Pico de Gallo, after learning that jalapeño peppers used as ingredients may have been contaminated with Salmonella. The affected products were distributed in Arkansas, Oklahoma, and Texas.


The U.S. Food and Drug Administration listed the recall in an Aug. 28 enforcement notice. According to recall information, the products were originally withdrawn on Aug. 6 and were later classified as a Class I recall, the most serious category used by the FDA.


## What Products Are Included?


The recall involves two products made by Ron's Home Style Foods.


The company recalled approximately 2,270 pounds of Salsa Autentica and another 2,270 pounds of Pico de Gallo. Both products were sold in five-pound, round plastic containers.


The affected items are identified as:


- Salsa Autentica, item number DIPSAU0205RFS
- Pico de Gallo, item number DIPPIC0205RFS


The company's product information identifies Salsa Autentica as a tomato-based salsa containing jalapeño peppers, among other ingredients. The product is sold in five-pound containers.


Consumers and businesses that may have purchased these products should check their containers carefully before serving or consuming them.


## Why Were the Products Recalled?


The concern centers on jalapeño peppers used during production.


According to the recall information, the products were made with jalapeños that had the potential to be contaminated with Salmonella. The recall is part of a broader series of actions involving fresh jalapeños that federal authorities have linked to a multistate Salmonella investigation.


The FDA says its investigation has resulted in additional recalls involving products made with or repackaged from the affected jalapeños. Other recalled foods have included salsa, guacamole, pico de gallo, dips, prepared foods, and other products containing the peppers.


The broader investigation has focused on jalapeños from Sinaloa, Mexico, that were distributed by Coast Citrus Distributors.


This means the Ron's Home Style Foods recall is part of a larger food-safety response rather than an isolated concern involving only salsa.


## What Does a Class I Recall Mean?


The FDA uses different classifications to communicate the potential severity of a recall.


A Class I recall represents the highest level of concern. It is used when there is a reasonable probability that consuming or being exposed to a recalled product could result in serious health consequences or death.


That classification does not mean that every person who consumes the product will become sick. Instead, it indicates that the potential health consequences are considered serious enough for the FDA to place the recall in its highest risk category.


Class II recalls generally involve situations in which exposure could cause temporary or medically reversible health effects. Class III recalls typically involve products that are unlikely to cause adverse health consequences, such as certain regulatory or labeling violations.


For consumers, the practical message is straightforward: recalled food should not be eaten.


## Salmonella Outbreak Adds to Concern


The recall comes as federal health officials continue investigating a Salmonella outbreak associated with jalapeño peppers.


The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention reported in early August that illnesses involving the outbreak strain had been identified across multiple states. At that time, the agency reported 345 illnesses in 27 states and 36 hospitalizations.


The CDC said traceback information indicated that the jalapeños were grown in Sinaloa, Mexico, and distributed by Coast Citrus Distributors.


As the investigation progressed, federal agencies identified additional products that may have been made using the recalled peppers. The FDA has warned consumers not to eat recalled jalapeños or foods made with them and has advised businesses not to sell or serve affected products.


Other companies have also issued recalls involving foods that contained the potentially contaminated peppers. For example, FDA records show recalls involving products sold through grocery retailers and food-service businesses, including various salsas, guacamole products, dips, and pico de gallo.


## What Should Consumers Do?


Anyone who believes they purchased the recalled Ron's Home Style Foods products should avoid eating them.


Consumers should not taste a product to determine whether it is safe. Food contaminated with Salmonella may look, smell, or taste normal.


If the recalled product is in a refrigerator, consumers should keep it away from other foods while determining how to dispose of it. Surfaces or containers that may have come into contact with recalled food should also be cleaned and sanitized.


Restaurants, caterers, retailers, and other food-service businesses should check their inventory as well. Any recalled products should not be served or sold.


The FDA has also advised businesses handling recalled jalapeños or products containing them to clean and sanitize surfaces and equipment that may have come into contact with the contaminated ingredients.


## What Are the Symptoms of Salmonella?


Salmonella infection can cause gastrointestinal symptoms that may develop several hours to several days after exposure.


Common symptoms include diarrhea, fever, and stomach cramps. According to the CDC, symptoms generally begin six hours to six days after exposure, and most people recover within four to seven days.


However, Salmonella infections can become more serious in some people. Young children, older adults, and individuals with weakened immune systems are at greater risk of severe illness.


Anyone who develops significant symptoms after eating a recalled product should contact a health professional for medical advice. People experiencing severe or worsening symptoms should seek prompt medical attention.


## A Wider Food-Safety Investigation


The Ron's Home Style Foods recall illustrates how contamination in a single ingredient can lead to recalls across multiple types of food.


Jalapeños are commonly used in salsa, pico de gallo, guacamole, sauces, salads, sandwiches, bowls, burritos, and other prepared foods. When contaminated ingredients enter the commercial food supply, manufacturers and retailers may need to recall finished products that used those ingredients.


The FDA's current investigation shows that additional recalls can occur as investigators trace the distribution of affected peppers and identify companies that used them.


Consumers therefore should not assume that a product is safe simply because it does not contain whole jalapeño peppers. Processed foods can also be affected when recalled ingredients are incorporated into their recipes.


## The Bottom Line


Consumers in Arkansas, Oklahoma, and Texas should check for the recalled five-pound containers of Ron's Home Style Foods Salsa Autentica and Pico de Gallo.


The recall covers approximately 4,540 pounds of product because the jalapeños used in manufacturing may have been contaminated with Salmonella. The products have been classified as a Class I recall, reflecting the potential seriousness of Salmonella exposure.


The recall is also connected to a broader federal investigation involving jalapeños distributed from Sinaloa, Mexico. As that investigation continues, consumers should pay attention to additional recall notices involving foods containing the affected peppers.


When in doubt, consumers should check the FDA's recall information and avoid consuming any product identified as recalled.


### Sources


U.S. Food and Drug Administration and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. The Ron's Home Style Foods product information was also reviewed through the company's published product listing.


### Disclaimer


This article is provided for general informational purposes and is not a substitute for official recall notices, medical advice, or instructions from public-health authorities. Recall information can change as federal investigations develop. Consumers should verify the latest product details, distribution information, and instructions directly with the FDA, CDC, or the relevant manufacturer before making decisions about recalled food.
